Every run of the harness should start with what it needs to work on a Piton
project, and a small, predictable context rather than an old transcript.

1. Piton fluency in every mode. [ModeSystemPromptsScope](.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/ModeSystemPromptsScope.md) gains a third

stands for the output of `piton claude --print-prompt`, run in the project
directory. It is run once when the project is opened and kept for as long as
it stays open. Where `piton` isn't installed or fails, it is replaced with
nothing, and the run goes ahead without it. Every mode's default template
(Code, Chain, Spec, and Ask) ends with PITON_FLUENCY, and like the other
placeholders it can be moved or removed in [SettingsWindowScope](.claude/reference/scope/settings-window/SettingsWindowScope.md). Projects
whose saved templates predate it keep them as they are.

2. Following references. Every mode's default template also says: "Links to
.claude/reference/… in the prompt are the spec for what they name. Read each
one before changing anything it covers."

3. Starting a new conversation. Tasks and questions each carry on their own
conversation, as [HarnessIntegrationScope](.claude/reference/scope/harness-integration/HarnessIntegrationScope.md) says. Add a "New conversation"
button to [ChatInputScope](.claude/reference/scope/prompt-mode/chat-input/ChatInputScope.md), at the right end of the help text beside the
tabs, that starts a new conversation for the selected tab: tasks for Code,
Chain, and Spec, questions for Ask. The next run in that tab starts fresh
instead of carrying on. Its tooltip says which conversation it resets. It is
disabled while that conversation has nothing to carry on, and while a run in
it is under way. The choice survives reopening the project, so a project
opened after its conversation was reset starts fresh too, rather than
carrying on the latest conversation in its history.

# Mode System Prompts Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

The system prompt each mode sends, which tells the harness what kind of work a prompt is, and which each project can make its own.

### Shape

#### Description

Each of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/PromptModesScope.md) has a system prompt template. A prompt sent in a mode gives its hidden anchor a systemPrompt property, alongside its userPrompt, from that mode's template.

#### Templates

A template is Piton prose, like the prompt it is sent with, so it can reference the spec, with two placeholders, CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION, each written after a dollar sign and inside braces like a Piton interpolation. Before the prompt is compiled, they are filled in with the code location and the spec location, as the [ProjectLocationsScope](../../project-locations/ProjectLocationsScope.md) says.

#### Saving

Each project has its own templates, saved with its data, as the [ProjectDataScope](../../project-data/ProjectDataScope.md) says, a Markdown file per mode, and edited in the [SettingsWindowScope](../../settings-window/SettingsWindowScope.md). A mode with no file yet sends its default.

#### Defaults

The defaults are the templates saved in this application's own repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, one Markdown file per mode, named as a project's are. They are the source of truth for the defaults, and are baked into the application when it is built, so a build always ships with whatever those files say, and changing them changes the defaults the next build has. A build can't be made without them.
The defaults are only where a project starts, and what resetting a template puts back.

Links in this document point at reference files. Read one when the work touches what it describes.

# Harness Integration Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

Uses the one-off version for a coding harness for the selected ProjectDirectoryScope. For example, `claude -p`. Each run carries on a conversation, so the harness keeps its context between requests.

### Shape

#### Description

Should always run in auto mode.
The compiled systemPrompt of a prompt's hidden anchor is appended to the harness's own system prompt, for example with `--append-system-prompt`.
The prompt is given to the harness on its standard input, and what the harness does is streamed back as it happens.

#### Context

The harness keeps its context between requests instead of starting fresh each time. Tasks share one ongoing conversation, and each task sent carries it on. When the project is opened, tasks carry on the latest conversation in its history. Questions from the Ask tab share a separate conversation of their own, and when the project is opened they carry on the latest conversation among the questions saved with it. A question asked while another is running carries on a copy of that conversation, so questions running at the same time never write over each other. A conversation is only carried on in the project it began in, each open project keeping its own tasks' and questions' conversations while it is in the background, and if one can't be carried on, the next request starts a new one. Each run applies its own prompt's systemPrompt, even when it carries on a conversation begun in a different mode. The palette's file search always starts fresh.
A conversation can be left for a new one, from the chat input's New Session, as the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/ChatInputScope.md) says: the next request starts a new conversation with no context, and the one left is not carried on again, not by a run of it still going, nor by the project's history, until the application is next opened. How much context a conversation holds is known from what the harness reports with each reply: everything the model was given, cached or not, and what it wrote, as of its latest reply; replies of subagents don't count.

#### Baked Prompts

[BakedSystemPromptsScope](baked-prompts/BakedSystemPromptsScope.md)

#### One Off Runs

[OneOffAgentRunScope](one-off-run/OneOffAgentRunScope.md)

#### Catalog

[HarnessCatalogScope](catalog/HarnessCatalogScope.md)

#### Mode System Prompts

[ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/ModeSystemPromptsScope.md)

Links in this document point at reference files. Read one when the work touches what it describes.

# Chat Input Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

A multi-line, syntax-highlighted textbox that accepts plain text as well as snippets of Piton.

### Shape

#### Description

Input on the left, send button on the right.
<Enter> allows for creating new lines, like Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it to the HarnessIntegrationScope
Sending sends the prompt in the selected tab's mode, as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/PromptSendingScope.md) says. While the harness is working, the send button on the Code, Chain, and Spec tabs reads "Queue", since the prompt will queue. On the Ask tab it always reads "Send", because a question is never queued. The button is only disabled while the input is empty.

#### Instructions

- [ChatInputInstruction](../../../shape/ChatInputInstruction.md)

#### Send Options

##### Split Button

The send button is a split button: the send or queue button itself, and joined to its right, a narrow half with a chevron that opens a menu of other ways to send the prompt, above the button, its right edge lined up with the button's. The chevron half is disabled whenever the send half is, and while a preview shows, and its tooltip says it shows more ways to send, with its shortcut.

##### Keyboard

<Ctrl+Shift+Enter> (<Cmd+Shift+Enter> on macOS) in the chat input opens the menu with its first option highlighted, and does nothing while the input is empty or a preview shows. While it is open, the text keeps focus, <Up> and <Down> move the highlight, wrapping around, <Enter> picks the highlighted option, and <Escape> closes the menu, as does pressing <Ctrl+Shift+Enter> again or the mouse anywhere outside it. Each option highlights on hover, and clicking one picks it.

##### Options

The menu's options, in order:

- "Preview Compiled Prompt", with an eye icon
- "Queue", with a list icon, which queues the prompt rather than sending it, even while the harness is free, as the queue of the [PromptEditor](../PromptEditor.md) says; like the send button, it clears the input. On the Ask tab it is disabled, since a question never queues, and the highlight passes over it

#### Editing Queued

Editing a queued prompt, from the queue of the [PromptEditor](../PromptEditor.md), sets aside the prompt being written, its attachments, and the selected tab, and puts the queued prompt's text in the input, its attachments above it, and its mode's tab selected, with the cursor at the end of the text. Above the attachments, a row with a pencil icon reads "Editing queued prompt N", its place in the queue, and at its right, muted, "Ctrl+Enter to save · Esc to cancel" (with ⌘ on macOS). The send button reads "Save", its tooltip saying it saves the queued prompt, and the send menu isn't offered.
Everything in the input works as ever while editing, tabs included. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS), or Save, saves the edit, in the tab selected then, and <Escape>, when nothing else in the input takes it, cancels it. Either way, the prompt that was set aside comes back just as it was. Saving an empty prompt isn't possible, just as sending one isn't. Editing another queued prompt meanwhile first cancels the edit in progress; so does switching projects.

#### Preview

Preview Compiled Prompt compiles the prompt as it would be sent from the selected tab, its hidden anchor, attachments, and mode's system prompt included, without sending it, saving it to the history, or building the spec first. In place of the text input, the chat input then shows what the harness would receive: the compiled prompt, as a sent task's compiled prompt is shown, beneath a row reading "Compiled prompt" with, at its right, muted, "Ctrl+Enter to send · Esc to edit" (with ⌘ on macOS). While it compiles, the row shows a spinner and "Compiling…"; a prompt that fails to compile shows why, in the theme's error colour, in place of the compiled prompt. The preview grows with what it shows, up to 40% of the window's height, and scrolls beyond that. The tabs, attachments, and send button stay as they are.
The preview has keyboard focus. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS), or the send button, sends the prompt just as sending from the text input would, and the chat input goes back to an empty text input. <Escape> goes back to the text input with the prompt and attachments as they were, the cursor where it was. Switching tabs while previewing goes back to the text input too, since the prompt would compile differently.

#### Tabs

```
overview: The input and send button live inside the body of a tab bar, using gpui-kit's default tab styling. There is a tab for each of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/PromptModesScope.md), in their order: Code, Chain, Spec, and Ask. Code, Spec, and Ask are ordinary tabs. Chain is also a tab, just a small one, because it only shows an icon. All four sit flush against each other with no extra gaps, and no tab has more padding than a normal tab.
The chat input starts in the combined mode: Chain is selected, so Code and Spec are selected together, and a prompt sent before switching tabs changes the code and the spec together.
Pressing <Ctrl+Tab> while in the chat input cycles from Code to Chain to Spec to Ask and back to Code, <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> the other way, and focus remains in the chat input. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too, not <Cmd>.
<Tab> and <Shift+Tab> don't switch tabs, and don't indent the text either: they move keyboard focus out of the chat input to the next or previous control, as they do everywhere else. While the completion menu is open, <Tab> is still the menu's.
chain: Chain is a tab with unusual behaviour. It shows an icon rather than a label, reading "Code and Spec" as its tooltip, and selecting it selects both Code and Spec. It never shows a focus outline, and its icon looks evenly spaced between Code and Spec whichever of the two is selected.
Unselected, it shows a broken chain dimmed to 50% opacity, and sits between Code and Spec like any other tab, overlapping neither of them.
In combined mode, with Chain selected, Chain has no line along its bottom, just as the joined Code and Spec beneath it have none. In separate mode, unselected, it has one, like any other unselected tab: the tab bar's bottom line runs beneath it, the same colour and thickness, in the same place, as beneath any other unselected tab, at any display scale. This holds at every window size and display scale, in light and dark mode: in combined mode nothing draws a line beneath Chain at all, rather than a line being drawn and then hidden, since a hidden line can show again wherever rounding to the display's pixels uncovers it.
Selected, it shows a joined chain at full opacity. Selecting it animates as though it took a margin of -50% of its own width on both its left and right sides: Code and Spec slide together until they meet underneath it, so it ends up sitting on top of both. Deselecting it animates them apart again. While Chain is selected, Code and Spec both show as selected and read as a single unified tab, with no line between them. Chain itself has a transparent background and no left or right borders, so the joined Code and Spec show through underneath it.
help: To the right of the tabs, filling the rest of the bar, a line of help text says what the selected tab is for, and changes as soon as another tab is selected. It is extra small and dimmer than muted text, set a little apart from the last tab, so it reads as a quiet note about the tab rather than as another tab. It is cut off rather than wrapped when the bar is too narrow.
It reads what the selected tab's mode is for, as the [PromptModesScope](../modes/PromptModesScope.md) says.
session: At the far right of the bar, after the help text, sits how much context the selected tab's conversation holds, then a New Session button. The questions of the Ask tab have a conversation of their own, and the other tabs share the tasks', as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/HarnessIntegrationScope.md) says, so the figure is the Ask tab's conversation while it is selected, and the tasks' on any other tab.
The figure reads "Context", then the number of tokens, short and extra small, muted: "850", "42.1k", "123k", or "1.2M", to a decimal place below a hundred of a unit. It follows each reply as the harness reports it. While the next prompt would start a new conversation, as when the project has none yet or New Session was just pressed, it reads "Context 0". Its tooltip says how many tokens the conversation the next prompt carries on holds, or that the next prompt starts a new conversation.
New Session is a small ghost button with a sparkles icon. Pressing it leaves the selected tab's conversation: the next prompt sent from that tab, or from any tab sharing its conversation, starts a new one with no context, and the figure reads "Context 0". A run of the conversation left that is still going finishes as it would, but neither it nor the project's history brings that conversation back. While there is no conversation to leave, it is disabled, and its tooltip says the next prompt already starts a new conversation.
Both sit on the bar's bottom line, which runs beneath them as it does beneath the help text, and neither is cut off: the help text gives way to them when the bar is narrow.
colour: The selected tab and the tab body holding the input are tinted the colour of its mode, of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/PromptModesScope.md). With Chain selected, Code, Spec, and the body are all purple. The colour transitions smoothly whenever the selected tab changes, straight from the old tab's colour to the new one's. The tabs wrap around, so pressing <Ctrl+Tab> on Ask fades green straight to Code's red, and <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> on Code fades red straight to Ask's green; neither lights up Chain or Spec on the way.
```

#### System Prompt

The selected tab is the mode a prompt is sent in, and each mode's system prompt is sent with it, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../mode-system-prompts/ModeSystemPromptsScope.md) says.

#### Ask

Ask is for simply asking a question, which runs as the [PromptModesScope](../modes/PromptModesScope.md) says. Any number of questions can be asked, and they all run at the same time; asking another never stops or waits for one already running.
Each question's progress and results are shown in a [TaskTableScope](../../../ui/components/task-table/TaskTableScope.md). The questions stack directly above the tabs, the newest nearest them, in a column that pushes the message list up to make room rather than covering it, so none of a running task's progress is ever hidden behind them. Each slides up out of the chat input with an animation as it is asked, the message list giving way above it. While the harness works on a question, it is a single row showing the latest thing the harness did. A finished question is a row with its status and first line.
Once a question is complete, it opens onto a heading, with its status and first line, above its full task table, in the [AnswerDrawerScope](../answer-drawer/AnswerDrawerScope.md), which it fills, the table scrolling once it is taller, with its lock to the bottom off to start with. Only one question is open at a time: opening another closes the one open back down to its row. An open question leaves the stack for the drawer. Clicking an open question's heading closes it down to its row in the stack, and clicking a finished question's row opens it again. Each question has a close button, which removes it and stops it if it is still running, leaving the others running. A closed question becomes a previous answer.

#### Answer Steps

For a question, only the answer matters, so wherever a finished question's task table is shown, an open question and a previous answer, the table collapses the steps leading up to the answer, as the [TaskTableScope](../../../ui/components/task-table/TaskTableScope.md) says. A question closed into the previous answers starts collapsed again. Tasks are never collapsed like this: see the [MessageList](../message-list/MessageList.md).

#### Previous Answers

Previous answers are a [HistoryListScope](../../../ui/components/history-list/HistoryListScope.md), shown only while the Ask tab is selected, at the top of the questions stacked above the tabs. It lists every question asked before and closed: those saved with the project and those closed since. Its row reads "No previous answers", "1 previous answer", or "N previous answers", and while expanded, "Back to the questions". Expanded, the row and the list go into the [AnswerDrawerScope](../answer-drawer/AnswerDrawerScope.md), sliding up from on top of any question rows still in the stack. The questions asked from now on carry on the conversation the latest of them left off.

#### Answer Drawer

[AnswerDrawerScope](../answer-drawer/AnswerDrawerScope.md)

#### Selecting Answer Text

The text of an answer being viewed, in the answer drawer, whether an open question or a previous answer, can be selected by dragging across it, as any text can. A drag that selects text ending within the drawer shows a [SelectionPopoverScope](../../../ui/components/selection-popover/SelectionPopoverScope.md) with two buttons: "Copy", with a copy icon, and "Attach to prompt", with a paperclip icon.
Copy puts the selected text on the clipboard. Attach to prompt adds it to the prompt as an attachment. Either one clears the selection. The popover also closes when the drawer closes.

#### Attachments

What is attached to the prompt is listed above the text input, between the tabs and the input, one row per attachment in the order they were attached, and only while there is anything attached. An attached piece of text shows a quote icon, the text's first line cut off with an ellipsis, and, when it runs to more than one line, how many lines it has, muted, and at the right end a small button with a cross, whose tooltip says it removes the attachment, which removes just that one.
Attachments belong to the prompt being written, not to a tab: switching tabs keeps them all, and they go with the prompt whichever tab it is sent from. When the prompt is sent, its attachments are sent along with it and the list empties, as the text input does. A queued prompt keeps the attachments it was sent with.

#### Projects

The questions stacked above the tabs, the open answer, and the previous answers belong to their project, as the [OpenProjectsScope](../../open-projects/OpenProjectsScope.md) says: switching projects shows those of the project switched to, while the questions of other projects carry on running in the background. The prompt being written, its attachments, and the selected tab stay as they are across a switch, and are sent to the project on screen.

#### Escape

Pressing <Escape> while in the chat input takes focus out of the chat input.

#### Grow To Fit

The text input is a [GrowingTextInputScope](../../../ui/components/growing-text-input/GrowingTextInputScope.md) growing to 12 rows at most. Its single row lines up with the send button.

#### Auto Focus

The chat input should be auto-focused.

#### Syntax Highlighting

Syntax highlighting will be supported via the [Tree Sitter Grammar](https://github.com/piton-lang/tree-sitter-piton)

#### Lsp

[LSP](../../lsp/LSP.md)

#### Harness Mentions

```
overview: Typing `/` offers the harness's skills and commands, and typing `@` offers its agents, the way they are offered in the harness itself. The placeholder mentions both.
trigger: A mention starts at `/` or `@` at the start of the input or after whitespace, so paths and email addresses never open it, and an at sign followed by an opening curly brace is still a Piton reference. Completions are requested after typing the `/` or `@`, and after each letter, digit, hyphen, underscore, or colon of the name that follows. Only inside a mention are a slash or a hyphen a trigger; outside of one they never reach the [LSP](../../lsp/LSP.md).
offered: The skills, commands, and agents offered are the [HarnessCatalogScope](../../harness-integration/catalog/HarnessCatalogScope.md)'s. Each shows whether it is a skill, command, or agent, and its description as documentation when it has one. Results are narrowed and ordered like Piton completions: matches at the start of a name before matches anywhere in it, then by name.
accepting: Accepting one inserts it as a mention, as the [HarnessCatalogScope](../../harness-integration/catalog/HarnessCatalogScope.md) says, in place of what was typed of it. Mentions work without the [LSP](../../lsp/LSP.md).
```

#### Hidden Anchor

While the user will be able to type plain text, behind the scenes, they'll be typing into a randomly-named piton anchor with a userPrompt property.  It's this compiled anchor that will be send to the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/HarnessIntegrationScope.md)

##### Escaping

A prompt may hold anything, text pasted into it included, so it isn't written into the anchor as Piton prose, where braces, quotes, colons, leading dashes, code fences, comments, indentation, and backslashes all mean something. Its userPrompt is a list with an item per line of the prompt, in order, and each line a list of its pieces: the text between references as a quoted string, with quotes, backslashes, and each dollar-brace escaped, so nothing in it is interpolated or evaluated; and each at-brace or dollar-brace around a dotted path of identifiers whose first name is imported as a reference of its own. A reference to a name that isn't imported, such as a pasted shell variable, is only text. An empty line is a single empty string. The compiled userPrompt is the pieces of each line joined together, and the lines joined by line breaks, so what the harness receives is exactly what was typed or pasted, line for line, with each reference resolved. The systemPrompt is written the same way. A prompt saved as prose by an earlier version still reads back.

##### Auto Imports

The names a prompt uses are imported however the prompt got there, typed, completed, or pasted. What `piton lsp` is shown while the prompt is typed is the prompt as prose, line for line and position for position as typed, but with anything outside a reference other than letters, digits, and spaces between words blanked out, character for character. Pasted text with an unclosed quote or brace, a code fence, deeper indentation, or what would be a comment then never stops the server finding the names that need importing, both as completions are offered and when the prompt is sent.

##### Attached Text

A prompt with attached text gives the hidden anchor an attachedText property: a list with an item per attached piece of text, in the order they were attached. Since attached text is taken as it is, not as Piton, each item is itself a list of the text's lines, each a quoted string, with quotes and backslashes escaped, so nothing in it is interpolated or evaluated. A prompt with nothing attached has no attachedText property.
What the harness receives is the compiled userPrompt followed by the attached text: a line reading "Attached text:", then each piece as a fenced code block, whose fence is longer than any run of backticks in the text itself. This is also the compiled prompt shown in the task's header.

## Theme

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../../ui/theme/ThemeScope.md): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

Links in this document point at reference files. Read one when the work touches what it describes.

# Settings Window Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

The application's settings, which for now are the system prompts each tab of the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/ChatInputScope.md) sends.

### Shape

#### Description

Shown in an [InsetPanelScope](../../ui/components/inset-panel/InsetPanelScope.md) over the main window, not a window of its own. It is headed "Settings", with a close button whose tooltip says it closes the settings; closing the panel any way an inset panel closes closes them too. Beneath the heading, its page scrolls with a [ScrollbarScope](../../ui/components/scrollbar/ScrollbarScope.md).

#### Opening

It opens with Ctrl+, (Cmd+, on macOS) from anywhere in the application, or from whatever command opens the settings, in place of anything else in the inset panel. Opening it while it is already open leaves it as it is rather than opening another.

#### System Prompts

The page is headed "System prompts", with a muted line beneath saying that each tab gives a prompt sent from it this system prompt, that they are saved with the project as they are edited, and that the CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION placeholders stand for the code and spec locations, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/ModeSystemPromptsScope.md) says.
Then, for each tab, in the order of the [PromptModesScope](../prompt-mode/modes/PromptModesScope.md): its name, the muted path of the file its prompt is saved in, and a "Reset to default" button, disabled while the prompt is already the default, which puts the default back and saves it. Beneath them, an editor for the prompt, 120 pixels tall before it scrolls, highlighting it as Piton, with soft wrapping and no line numbers or folding. A prompt that can't be read or saved says why beneath its editor.
Without a project open, as the [NoProjectStateScope](../no-project/NoProjectStateScope.md) says, in place of the prompts it reads "Open a project to edit its system prompts."

#### Saving

The prompts belong to the project opened through the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../project-directory/ProjectDirectoryScope.md), each saved with the project's data, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/ProjectDataScope.md) says. Every edit is saved straight away. When the window loads the prompts, any tab with no file yet has its default saved, so every prompt can also be found and edited by hand. The prompts are read again each time the settings open and whenever another project is opened, so an edit made by hand shows up; a prompt that already shows what was read is left alone, so its cursor stays put.

#### Templates

A prompt is a template, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/ModeSystemPromptsScope.md) says, and a reset puts back its default.

## Theme

# Harness Integration Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

Uses the one-off version for a coding harness for the selected ProjectDirectoryScope. For example, `claude -p`. Each run carries on a conversation, so the harness keeps its context between requests.

### Shape

#### Description

Should always run in auto mode.
The compiled systemPrompt of a prompt's hidden anchor is appended to the harness's own system prompt, for example with `--append-system-prompt`.
The prompt is given to the harness on its standard input, and what the harness does is streamed back as it happens.

#### Context

The harness keeps its context between requests instead of starting fresh each time. Tasks share one ongoing conversation, and each task sent carries it on. When the project is opened, tasks carry on the latest conversation in its history. Questions from the Ask tab share a separate conversation of their own, and when the project is opened they carry on the latest conversation among the questions saved with it. A question asked while another is running carries on a copy of that conversation, so questions running at the same time never write over each other. A conversation is only carried on in the project it began in, each open project keeping its own tasks' and questions' conversations while it is in the background, and if one can't be carried on, the next request starts a new one. Each run applies its own prompt's systemPrompt, even when it carries on a conversation begun in a different mode. The palette's file search always starts fresh.
A conversation can be left for a new one, from the chat input's New Session, as the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/ChatInputScope.md) says: the next request starts a new conversation with no context, and the one left is not carried on again, not by a run of it still going, nor by the project's history, until the application is next opened. How much context a conversation holds is known from what the harness reports with each reply: everything the model was given, cached or not, and what it wrote, as of its latest reply; replies of subagents don't count.

# Chat Input Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

A multi-line, syntax-highlighted textbox that accepts plain text as well as snippets of Piton.

### Shape

#### Description

Input on the left, send button on the right.
<Enter> allows for creating new lines, like Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends it to the HarnessIntegrationScope
Sending sends the prompt in the selected tab's mode, as the [PromptSendingScope](../sending/PromptSendingScope.md) says. While the harness is working, the send button on the Code, Chain, and Spec tabs reads "Queue", since the prompt will queue. On the Ask tab it always reads "Send", because a question is never queued. The button is only disabled while the input is empty.

#### Instructions

- [ChatInputInstruction](../../../shape/ChatInputInstruction.md)

#### Send Options

##### Split Button

The send button is a split button: the send or queue button itself, and joined to its right, a narrow half with a chevron that opens a menu of other ways to send the prompt, above the button, its right edge lined up with the button's. The chevron half is disabled whenever the send half is, and while a preview shows, and its tooltip says it shows more ways to send, with its shortcut.

##### Keyboard

<Ctrl+Shift+Enter> (<Cmd+Shift+Enter> on macOS) in the chat input opens the menu with its first option highlighted, and does nothing while the input is empty or a preview shows. While it is open, the text keeps focus, <Up> and <Down> move the highlight, wrapping around, <Enter> picks the highlighted option, and <Escape> closes the menu, as does pressing <Ctrl+Shift+Enter> again or the mouse anywhere outside it. Each option highlights on hover, and clicking one picks it.

##### Options

The menu's options, in order:

- "Preview Compiled Prompt", with an eye icon
- "Queue", with a list icon, which queues the prompt rather than sending it, even while the harness is free, as the queue of the [PromptEditor](../PromptEditor.md) says; like the send button, it clears the input. On the Ask tab it is disabled, since a question never queues, and the highlight passes over it

#### Editing Queued

Editing a queued prompt, from the queue of the [PromptEditor](../PromptEditor.md), sets aside the prompt being written, its attachments, and the selected tab, and puts the queued prompt's text in the input, its attachments above it, and its mode's tab selected, with the cursor at the end of the text. Above the attachments, a row with a pencil icon reads "Editing queued prompt N", its place in the queue, and at its right, muted, "Ctrl+Enter to save · Esc to cancel" (with ⌘ on macOS). The send button reads "Save", its tooltip saying it saves the queued prompt, and the send menu isn't offered.
Everything in the input works as ever while editing, tabs included. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS), or Save, saves the edit, in the tab selected then, and <Escape>, when nothing else in the input takes it, cancels it. Either way, the prompt that was set aside comes back just as it was. Saving an empty prompt isn't possible, just as sending one isn't. Editing another queued prompt meanwhile first cancels the edit in progress; so does switching projects.

#### Preview

Preview Compiled Prompt compiles the prompt as it would be sent from the selected tab, its hidden anchor, attachments, and mode's system prompt included, without sending it, saving it to the history, or building the spec first. In place of the text input, the chat input then shows what the harness would receive: the compiled prompt, as a sent task's compiled prompt is shown, beneath a row reading "Compiled prompt" with, at its right, muted, "Ctrl+Enter to send · Esc to edit" (with ⌘ on macOS). While it compiles, the row shows a spinner and "Compiling…"; a prompt that fails to compile shows why, in the theme's error colour, in place of the compiled prompt. The preview grows with what it shows, up to 40% of the window's height, and scrolls beyond that. The tabs, attachments, and send button stay as they are.
The preview has keyboard focus. <Ctrl+Enter> (<Cmd+Enter> on macOS), or the send button, sends the prompt just as sending from the text input would, and the chat input goes back to an empty text input. <Escape> goes back to the text input with the prompt and attachments as they were, the cursor where it was. Switching tabs while previewing goes back to the text input too, since the prompt would compile differently.

#### Tabs

```
overview: The input and send button live inside the body of a tab bar, using gpui-kit's default tab styling. There is a tab for each of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/PromptModesScope.md), in their order: Code, Chain, Spec, and Ask. Code, Spec, and Ask are ordinary tabs. Chain is also a tab, just a small one, because it only shows an icon. All four sit flush against each other with no extra gaps, and no tab has more padding than a normal tab.
The chat input starts in the combined mode: Chain is selected, so Code and Spec are selected together, and a prompt sent before switching tabs changes the code and the spec together.
Pressing <Ctrl+Tab> while in the chat input cycles from Code to Chain to Spec to Ask and back to Code, <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> the other way, and focus remains in the chat input. It is <Ctrl> on macOS too, not <Cmd>.
<Tab> and <Shift+Tab> don't switch tabs, and don't indent the text either: they move keyboard focus out of the chat input to the next or previous control, as they do everywhere else. While the completion menu is open, <Tab> is still the menu's.
chain: Chain is a tab with unusual behaviour. It shows an icon rather than a label, reading "Code and Spec" as its tooltip, and selecting it selects both Code and Spec. It never shows a focus outline, and its icon looks evenly spaced between Code and Spec whichever of the two is selected.
Unselected, it shows a broken chain dimmed to 50% opacity, and sits between Code and Spec like any other tab, overlapping neither of them.
In combined mode, with Chain selected, Chain has no line along its bottom, just as the joined Code and Spec beneath it have none. In separate mode, unselected, it has one, like any other unselected tab: the tab bar's bottom line runs beneath it, the same colour and thickness, in the same place, as beneath any other unselected tab, at any display scale. This holds at every window size and display scale, in light and dark mode: in combined mode nothing draws a line beneath Chain at all, rather than a line being drawn and then hidden, since a hidden line can show again wherever rounding to the display's pixels uncovers it.
Selected, it shows a joined chain at full opacity. Selecting it animates as though it took a margin of -50% of its own width on both its left and right sides: Code and Spec slide together until they meet underneath it, so it ends up sitting on top of both. Deselecting it animates them apart again. While Chain is selected, Code and Spec both show as selected and read as a single unified tab, with no line between them. Chain itself has a transparent background and no left or right borders, so the joined Code and Spec show through underneath it.
help: To the right of the tabs, filling the rest of the bar, a line of help text says what the selected tab is for, and changes as soon as another tab is selected. It is extra small and dimmer than muted text, set a little apart from the last tab, so it reads as a quiet note about the tab rather than as another tab. It is cut off rather than wrapped when the bar is too narrow.
It reads what the selected tab's mode is for, as the [PromptModesScope](../modes/PromptModesScope.md) says.
session: At the far right of the bar, after the help text, sits how much context the selected tab's conversation holds, then a New Session button. The questions of the Ask tab have a conversation of their own, and the other tabs share the tasks', as the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/HarnessIntegrationScope.md) says, so the figure is the Ask tab's conversation while it is selected, and the tasks' on any other tab.
The figure reads "Context", then the number of tokens, short and extra small, muted: "850", "42.1k", "123k", or "1.2M", to a decimal place below a hundred of a unit. It follows each reply as the harness reports it. While the next prompt would start a new conversation, as when the project has none yet or New Session was just pressed, it reads "Context 0". Its tooltip says how many tokens the conversation the next prompt carries on holds, or that the next prompt starts a new conversation.
New Session is a small ghost button with a sparkles icon. Pressing it leaves the selected tab's conversation: the next prompt sent from that tab, or from any tab sharing its conversation, starts a new one with no context, and the figure reads "Context 0". A run of the conversation left that is still going finishes as it would, but neither it nor the project's history brings that conversation back. While there is no conversation to leave, it is disabled, and its tooltip says the next prompt already starts a new conversation.
Both sit on the bar's bottom line, which runs beneath them as it does beneath the help text, and neither is cut off: the help text gives way to them when the bar is narrow.
colour: The selected tab and the tab body holding the input are tinted the colour of its mode, of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/PromptModesScope.md). With Chain selected, Code, Spec, and the body are all purple. The colour transitions smoothly whenever the selected tab changes, straight from the old tab's colour to the new one's. The tabs wrap around, so pressing <Ctrl+Tab> on Ask fades green straight to Code's red, and <Ctrl+Shift+Tab> on Code fades red straight to Ask's green; neither lights up Chain or Spec on the way.
```

#### System Prompt

The selected tab is the mode a prompt is sent in, and each mode's system prompt is sent with it, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../mode-system-prompts/ModeSystemPromptsScope.md) says.

#### Ask

Ask is for simply asking a question, which runs as the [PromptModesScope](../modes/PromptModesScope.md) says. Any number of questions can be asked, and they all run at the same time; asking another never stops or waits for one already running.
Each question's progress and results are shown in a [TaskTableScope](../../../ui/components/task-table/TaskTableScope.md). The questions stack directly above the tabs, the newest nearest them, in a column that pushes the message list up to make room rather than covering it, so none of a running task's progress is ever hidden behind them. Each slides up out of the chat input with an animation as it is asked, the message list giving way above it. While the harness works on a question, it is a single row showing the latest thing the harness did. A finished question is a row with its status and first line.
Once a question is complete, it opens onto a heading, with its status and first line, above its full task table, in the [AnswerDrawerScope](../answer-drawer/AnswerDrawerScope.md), which it fills, the table scrolling once it is taller, with its lock to the bottom off to start with. Only one question is open at a time: opening another closes the one open back down to its row. An open question leaves the stack for the drawer. Clicking an open question's heading closes it down to its row in the stack, and clicking a finished question's row opens it again. Each question has a close button, which removes it and stops it if it is still running, leaving the others running. A closed question becomes a previous answer.

#### Answer Steps

For a question, only the answer matters, so wherever a finished question's task table is shown, an open question and a previous answer, the table collapses the steps leading up to the answer, as the [TaskTableScope](../../../ui/components/task-table/TaskTableScope.md) says. A question closed into the previous answers starts collapsed again. Tasks are never collapsed like this: see the [MessageList](../message-list/MessageList.md).

#### Previous Answers

Previous answers are a [HistoryListScope](../../../ui/components/history-list/HistoryListScope.md), shown only while the Ask tab is selected, at the top of the questions stacked above the tabs. It lists every question asked before and closed: those saved with the project and those closed since. Its row reads "No previous answers", "1 previous answer", or "N previous answers", and while expanded, "Back to the questions". Expanded, the row and the list go into the [AnswerDrawerScope](../answer-drawer/AnswerDrawerScope.md), sliding up from on top of any question rows still in the stack. The questions asked from now on carry on the conversation the latest of them left off.

#### Answer Drawer

[AnswerDrawerScope](../answer-drawer/AnswerDrawerScope.md)

#### Selecting Answer Text

The text of an answer being viewed, in the answer drawer, whether an open question or a previous answer, can be selected by dragging across it, as any text can. A drag that selects text ending within the drawer shows a [SelectionPopoverScope](../../../ui/components/selection-popover/SelectionPopoverScope.md) with two buttons: "Copy", with a copy icon, and "Attach to prompt", with a paperclip icon.
Copy puts the selected text on the clipboard. Attach to prompt adds it to the prompt as an attachment. Either one clears the selection. The popover also closes when the drawer closes.

#### Attachments

What is attached to the prompt is listed above the text input, between the tabs and the input, one row per attachment in the order they were attached, and only while there is anything attached. An attached piece of text shows a quote icon, the text's first line cut off with an ellipsis, and, when it runs to more than one line, how many lines it has, muted, and at the right end a small button with a cross, whose tooltip says it removes the attachment, which removes just that one.
Attachments belong to the prompt being written, not to a tab: switching tabs keeps them all, and they go with the prompt whichever tab it is sent from. When the prompt is sent, its attachments are sent along with it and the list empties, as the text input does. A queued prompt keeps the attachments it was sent with.

#### Projects

The questions stacked above the tabs, the open answer, and the previous answers belong to their project, as the [OpenProjectsScope](../../open-projects/OpenProjectsScope.md) says: switching projects shows those of the project switched to, while the questions of other projects carry on running in the background. The prompt being written, its attachments, and the selected tab stay as they are across a switch, and are sent to the project on screen.

#### Escape

Pressing <Escape> while in the chat input takes focus out of the chat input.

#### Grow To Fit

The text input is a [GrowingTextInputScope](../../../ui/components/growing-text-input/GrowingTextInputScope.md) growing to 12 rows at most. Its single row lines up with the send button.

#### Auto Focus

The chat input should be auto-focused.

#### Syntax Highlighting

Syntax highlighting will be supported via the [Tree Sitter Grammar](https://github.com/piton-lang/tree-sitter-piton)

#### Lsp

[LSP](../../lsp/LSP.md)

#### Harness Mentions

```
overview: Typing `/` offers the harness's skills and commands, and typing `@` offers its agents, the way they are offered in the harness itself. The placeholder mentions both.
trigger: A mention starts at `/` or `@` at the start of the input or after whitespace, so paths and email addresses never open it, and an at sign followed by an opening curly brace is still a Piton reference. Completions are requested after typing the `/` or `@`, and after each letter, digit, hyphen, underscore, or colon of the name that follows. Only inside a mention are a slash or a hyphen a trigger; outside of one they never reach the [LSP](../../lsp/LSP.md).
offered: The skills, commands, and agents offered are the [HarnessCatalogScope](../../harness-integration/catalog/HarnessCatalogScope.md)'s. Each shows whether it is a skill, command, or agent, and its description as documentation when it has one. Results are narrowed and ordered like Piton completions: matches at the start of a name before matches anywhere in it, then by name.
accepting: Accepting one inserts it as a mention, as the [HarnessCatalogScope](../../harness-integration/catalog/HarnessCatalogScope.md) says, in place of what was typed of it. Mentions work without the [LSP](../../lsp/LSP.md).
```

#### Hidden Anchor

While the user will be able to type plain text, behind the scenes, they'll be typing into a randomly-named piton anchor with a userPrompt property.  It's this compiled anchor that will be send to the [HarnessIntegrationScope](../../harness-integration/HarnessIntegrationScope.md)

##### Escaping

A prompt may hold anything, text pasted into it included, so it isn't written into the anchor as Piton prose, where braces, quotes, colons, leading dashes, code fences, comments, indentation, and backslashes all mean something. Its userPrompt is a list with an item per line of the prompt, in order, and each line a list of its pieces: the text between references as a quoted string, with quotes, backslashes, and each dollar-brace escaped, so nothing in it is interpolated or evaluated; and each at-brace or dollar-brace around a dotted path of identifiers whose first name is imported as a reference of its own. A reference to a name that isn't imported, such as a pasted shell variable, is only text. An empty line is a single empty string. The compiled userPrompt is the pieces of each line joined together, and the lines joined by line breaks, so what the harness receives is exactly what was typed or pasted, line for line, with each reference resolved. The systemPrompt is written the same way. A prompt saved as prose by an earlier version still reads back.

##### Auto Imports

The names a prompt uses are imported however the prompt got there, typed, completed, or pasted. What `piton lsp` is shown while the prompt is typed is the prompt as prose, line for line and position for position as typed, but with anything outside a reference other than letters, digits, and spaces between words blanked out, character for character. Pasted text with an unclosed quote or brace, a code fence, deeper indentation, or what would be a comment then never stops the server finding the names that need importing, both as completions are offered and when the prompt is sent.

##### Attached Text

A prompt with attached text gives the hidden anchor an attachedText property: a list with an item per attached piece of text, in the order they were attached. Since attached text is taken as it is, not as Piton, each item is itself a list of the text's lines, each a quoted string, with quotes and backslashes escaped, so nothing in it is interpolated or evaluated. A prompt with nothing attached has no attachedText property.
What the harness receives is the compiled userPrompt followed by the attached text: a line reading "Attached text:", then each piece as a fenced code block, whose fence is longer than any run of backticks in the text itself. This is also the compiled prompt shown in the task's header.

Drawn in the [ThemeScope](../../../ui/theme/ThemeScope.md): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

# Settings Window Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

The application's settings, which for now are the system prompts each tab of the [ChatInputScope](../prompt-mode/chat-input/ChatInputScope.md) sends.

### Shape

#### Description

Shown in an [InsetPanelScope](../../ui/components/inset-panel/InsetPanelScope.md) over the main window, not a window of its own. It is headed "Settings", with a close button whose tooltip says it closes the settings; closing the panel any way an inset panel closes closes them too. Beneath the heading, its page scrolls with a [ScrollbarScope](../../ui/components/scrollbar/ScrollbarScope.md).

#### Opening

It opens with Ctrl+, (Cmd+, on macOS) from anywhere in the application, or from whatever command opens the settings, in place of anything else in the inset panel. Opening it while it is already open leaves it as it is rather than opening another.

#### System Prompts

The page is headed "System prompts", with a muted line beneath saying that each tab gives a prompt sent from it this system prompt, that they are saved with the project as they are edited, and that the CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION placeholders stand for the code and spec locations, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/ModeSystemPromptsScope.md) says.
Then, for each tab, in the order of the [PromptModesScope](../prompt-mode/modes/PromptModesScope.md): its name, the muted path of the file its prompt is saved in, and a "Reset to default" button, disabled while the prompt is already the default, which puts the default back and saves it. Beneath them, an editor for the prompt, 120 pixels tall before it scrolls, highlighting it as Piton, with soft wrapping and no line numbers or folding. A prompt that can't be read or saved says why beneath its editor.
Without a project open, as the [NoProjectStateScope](../no-project/NoProjectStateScope.md) says, in place of the prompts it reads "Open a project to edit its system prompts."

#### Saving

The prompts belong to the project opened through the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../project-directory/ProjectDirectoryScope.md), each saved with the project's data, as the [ProjectDataScope](../project-data/ProjectDataScope.md) says. Every edit is saved straight away. When the window loads the prompts, any tab with no file yet has its default saved, so every prompt can also be found and edited by hand. The prompts are read again each time the settings open and whenever another project is opened, so an edit made by hand shows up; a prompt that already shows what was read is left alone, so its cursor stays put.

#### Templates

A prompt is a template, as the [ModeSystemPromptsScope](../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts/ModeSystemPromptsScope.md) says, and a reset puts back its default.

use /lib
from /scope/prompt-mode/modes import PromptModesScope
from /scope/project-data import ProjectDataScope
from /scope/project-locations import ProjectLocationsScope
from /scope/settings-window import SettingsWindowScope

export scope ModeSystemPromptsScope:
    concept: {ModeSystemPromptsConcept}

concept ModeSystemPromptsConcept:
    pitch:
        The system prompt each mode sends, which tells the harness what kind of
        work a prompt is, and which each project can make its own.

    shape: {ModeSystemPromptsShape}

shape ModeSystemPromptsShape:
    description:
        Each of the @{PromptModesScope} has a system prompt template. A prompt
        sent in a mode gives its hidden anchor a systemPrompt property,
        alongside its userPrompt, from that mode's template.

    templates:
        A template is Piton prose, like the prompt it is sent with, so it can
        reference the spec, with two placeholders, CODE_LOCATION and
        SPEC_LOCATION, each written after a dollar sign and inside braces like a
        Piton interpolation. Before the prompt is compiled, they are filled in
        with the code location and the spec location, as the
        @{ProjectLocationsScope} says.

    saving:
        Each project has its own templates, saved with its data, as the
        @{ProjectDataScope} says, a Markdown file per mode, and edited in the
        @{SettingsWindowScope}. A mode with no file yet sends its default.

    defaults:
        The defaults are the templates saved in this application's own
        repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, one Markdown
        file per mode, named as a project's are. They are the source of truth
        for the defaults, and are baked into the application when it is built,
        so a build always ships with whatever those files say, and changing
        them changes the defaults the next build has. A build can't be made
        without them.

        The defaults are only where a project starts, and what resetting a
        template puts back.
#####
use /lib
from ../project-directory import ProjectDirectoryScope
from ./baked-prompts import BakedSystemPromptsScope
from ./catalog import HarnessCatalogScope
from ./one-off-run import OneOffAgentRunScope
from ../prompt-mode/mode-system-prompts import ModeSystemPromptsScope
from /scope/prompt-mode/chat-input import ChatInputScope

export scope HarnessIntegrationScope:
    concept: {HarnessIntegrationConcept}

concept HarnessIntegrationConcept:
    pitch:
        Uses the one-off version for a coding harness for the selected

# Piton fluency

Piton is a declarative, whitespace-structured language for describing agentic
skills, agents, commands, and reference documents. It has no runtime: it
compiles to data (JSON, YAML) or, through a framework, to Markdown. Source
files use the `.pi` extension.

## Syntax

```piton
// A comment. Comments are line-only.
myVariable: 42                       // a number
myString: Strings are unquoted       // a string
myQuoted: "false"                    // quoting forces a string
myTyped:: string:: number: 42        // constraints, first match wins

myList:
    - one
    - two
myInlineList: [one, two, three]

myDictionary:
    nested:
        deep: value

computed: {1 + 2}                    // `{ }` evaluates; bare text does not
interpolated: Hello, ${myString}

anchor Base:
    name: Base
    summary: This is ${this.name}  // `this` pins to Base

anchor Child extends Base:
    name: Child
    detail: This is ${self.name}   // `self` follows the child
    summary: ${super.summary} and more

abstract anchor Shape as shape:      // `as` registers a keyword
    description:: string

shape Concrete:                      // same as `extends Shape`
    description: Implemented

from ./other import Thing, Other Alias
from ./other export *
use ./keywords
export anchor Published:
    value: 1
```

## Reserved words

`anchor`, `abstract`, `extends`, `as`, `export`, `from`, `import`, `use`, `this`, `self`, `super`, `true`, `false`, `null`

## Types

`string`, `number`, `boolean`, `null`, `list`, `dictionary`, `anchor`, `any`, `simple`, `complex`

Literals: `true`, `false`, `null`

## Rules worth memorising

- A value is an expression only when the *whole* value parses as one over
  literal atoms. `1 + 2` is `3`; `a + b` is the string `a + b`; use `{a + b}`
  to reference names.
- `+` on lists concatenates and deduplicates, right operand winning:
  `[1,2,3,4] + [1,2,3]` is `[4,1,2,3]`. `++` keeps duplicates.
- `+` merges dictionaries shallowly; `++` merges them deeply.
- Mixing unrelated types with `+` produces a mixed list, not an error.
- A block that mixes prose, `- ` items, and `key:` pairs becomes an implicit
  list; the keys written directly in it stay addressable.
- Inheritance is left to right with the right-most base winning; a child always
  wins over its bases; a declaring keyword is the left-most base.
- A concrete anchor may implement at most one abstract anchor, and must supply
  every abstract property left without a value.
- Strings never coerce to `boolean` or `number`; simple values do coerce to
  `string`.
- Modulo uses floor semantics; division by zero and comparing mismatched types
  are compile errors.
- Two files may import from each other. A circular reference is an error only
  when it cannot settle: `${A}` and `${B}` naming each other is fine, because an
  interpolated anchor renders as its name, while `A: {B}` and `B: {A}` is not.
- A `- ` item's text continues, as in Markdown, on the lines after it that
  are indented past its marker, joining with a space. The canonical alignment
  is two columns past the `-`, and a `key:` line there is text.
- Prose lines join with a space and a blank line starts a new line. A fenced
  code block, opened on an indented line by three or more backticks or tildes
  and closed by a line of at least as many of the same, is taken exactly as
  written instead: no comments, escapes, keys, or interpolations inside, its
  line breaks and relative indentation kept, its fences part of the string.
- `\` escapes the character after it, so `\\` is a backslash. A run of
  backslashes followed by a space opens an escape group that a space and the
  same run closes: `\ // not a comment \` is text, nothing inside it is read as
  Piton, the delimiters are not part of the string, and one more backslash on
  each side holds a shorter delimiter inside.
- Indentation must be consistent within a file; the canonical style is four
  spaces.

## Frameworks

### `@piton/belay` (framework `belay`)

`use @piton/belay` for its keywords, `from @piton/belay import ...` for its anchors.

Interpolation sigils: `@{}`

- **Agent** (abstract anchor) — keyword `agent`
  - `description:: string`
  - `role:: string`
  - `prompt:: string`
- **Skill** (abstract anchor) — keyword `skill`
  - `description:: string`
  - `prompt:: string`
  - `useWhen:: string`
- **Command** (abstract anchor) — keyword `command`
  - `description:: string`
  - `prompt:: string`
- **Instruction** (abstract anchor) — keyword `instruction`
  - `description:: string`
  - `prompt:: string`
- **SelfInstruction** (abstract anchor) — keyword `self-instruction`
  - `description:: string`
  - `prompt:: string`
- **BelayConfig** (abstract anchor) — keyword `belay-config`
  - `codeRoot:: string`
- **Adapter** (abstract anchor) — keyword `belay-adapter`
  - `description:: string`
- **AgentAdapter** (abstract anchor) — keyword `belay-agent-adapter`
  - `description:: string`
- **ClaudeAdapter** (anchor)
  - `description`
  - `claude`
- **OpenCodeAdapter** (anchor)
  - `description`
  - `opencode`
- **__BELAY_SHAPE__** (variable)

## Working with a Piton project

- `piton check <glob>` reports errors without writing anything.
- `piton compile <glob>` writes JSON or YAML next to each input.
- `piton build` builds the project described by `piton.config.pi`.
- `piton build check` builds and reports without writing.
- `piton format <glob>` applies the canonical style: four spaces, one space
  after `//`, sorted and wrapped import lists.
- `piton lsp` runs the language server.

## Writing Piton well

- Prefer an abstract anchor exported `as` a keyword for anything that will be
  implemented repeatedly; it documents intent and prevents a concrete anchor
  from implementing two abstracts.
- Reach for `+ {super.x}` rather than repeating a base's list.
- Use `this` when a base wants its own value and `self` when it wants the
  most-derived one.
- Keep prose as prose. Only reach for `{ }` when a value genuinely needs to be
  computed or referenced.

            it leaves the selected tab's conversation: the next prompt sent from
            that tab, or from any tab sharing its conversation, starts a new one
            with no context, and the figure reads "Context 0". A run of the

# Project Data Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

What the application keeps for a project, kept in the project itself so it survives a restart and travels with the project.

### Shape

#### Description

Everything the application keeps for a project lives in a `.suspense` directory inside the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../project-directory/ProjectDirectoryScope.md), created as it is needed. Nothing about a project is kept anywhere else, apart from the draft.

#### Contents

- `history/`: every task sent, as its hidden anchor's source, named by the second it was sent and the anchor's name, and beside it, once its run is over, a `.json` record of the same name holding the compiled userPrompt the harness received, each line the harness printed, and any error
- `asks/`: every question asked from the Ask tab, saved the same way as a task but apart from them
- `queue/`: each queued prompt, as its hidden anchor's source, imports included, named so they list in the order they were queued
- `divergence/`: each divergence report, a JSON file named by when it was made
- `system-prompts/`: each mode's system prompt template, a Markdown file named after its mode, code.md, combined.md for Chain, spec.md, and ask.md
- `commit-notes.json`: the Git panel's commit notes
- `harness.json`: the last report the harness gave of the skills and agents it has

The draft, `.suspense-draft.pi`, isn't in `.suspense`: it is the prompt being written, as `piton lsp` is shown it, a document named as if it were in the spec location, as the [ProjectLocationsScope](../project-locations/ProjectLocationsScope.md) says, so the server resolves its imports.

#### Machine Only

Some of it belongs to one machine rather than to the project: the harness report `.suspense/harness.json`, the queue `.suspense/queue/`, the commit notes `.suspense/commit-notes.json`, and the draft `.suspense-draft.pi` wherever it is, should it ever be written. Git ignores these, so they are never committed. Everything else, the prompt history, the questions, the divergence reports, and the system prompts, is kept with the project.

#### Reading

What can't be read is left out, or shown as missing, rather than stopping the rest from being read.

#### Last Project

When the application starts, it opens the project that was opened most recently, the first of the [ProjectDirectoryScope](../project-directory/ProjectDirectoryScope.md)'s recent projects that still holds its piton.config.pi. With none, it starts with no project open.

Links in this document point at reference files. Read one when the work touches what it describes.

# Mode System Prompts Scope

## Concept

### Pitch

The system prompt each mode sends, which tells the harness what kind of work a prompt is, and which each project can make its own.

### Shape

#### Description

Each of the [PromptModesScope](../modes/PromptModesScope.md) has a system prompt template. A prompt sent in a mode gives its hidden anchor a systemPrompt property, alongside its userPrompt, from that mode's template.

#### Templates

A template is Piton prose, like the prompt it is sent with, so it can reference the spec, with two placeholders, CODE_LOCATION and SPEC_LOCATION, each written after a dollar sign and inside braces like a Piton interpolation. Before the prompt is compiled, they are filled in with the code location and the spec location, as the [ProjectLocationsScope](../../project-locations/ProjectLocationsScope.md) says.

#### Saving

Each project has its own templates, saved with its data, as the [ProjectDataScope](../../project-data/ProjectDataScope.md) says, a Markdown file per mode, and edited in the [SettingsWindowScope](../../settings-window/SettingsWindowScope.md). A mode with no file yet sends its default.

#### Defaults

The defaults are the templates saved in this application's own repository, in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory, one Markdown file per mode, named as a project's are. They are the source of truth for the defaults, and are baked into the application when it is built, so a build always ships with whatever those files say, and changing them changes the defaults the next build has. A build can't be made without them.
The defaults are only where a project starts, and what resetting a template puts back.

Links in this document point at reference files. Read one when the work touches what it describes.

## Plan: Piton fluency, the reference-following line, and "New conversation"

**How it works today (dafc9fd).**
- **Resuming.** `Session { project_dir, id, context }` lives at `src/prompt_mode.rs:855`. `Session::resume` passes the id to `harness.rs:112`, which adds `--resume` (and `--fork-session` for a question started while another is running).
- **Finding the latest conversation.** `Session::latest(history, dir)` (`prompt_mode.rs:880`) takes the last session id found in the saved history. `load_history` (`:1752`) and `load_answers` (`:2116`) call it in the background when a project is first opened, from `project_changed` (`:1250`).
- **Leaving a conversation.** New Session emits `chat_input::NewSession` (`chat_input.rs:368`). `PromptMode::new_session` (`:2073`) sets the tab's conversation (`session` for tasks, `ask_session` for questions) to `None` and bumps an in-memory counter (`session_epoch` or `ask_session_epoch`). That counter stops late runs and the history loaders from bringing the old conversation back.
- **Not persisted.** A fresh launch has the counter back at 0, so `latest` resumes the old conversation again.
- **Button state.** It is disabled only when `context.is_none()` (`chat_input.rs:1340`). It is not disabled while a run is under way.
- **Where it sits.** It is already at the right end of the help text. The request's button replaces it, so I'd adapt this button rather than add a second one. The "Context N" figure stays as it is.

### 1. `src/piton_fluency.rs` (new) and `main.rs` / `app.rs` init
- Cache: a `static` `Mutex<HashMap<PathBuf, Arc<OnceLock<String>>>>`.
  - `pub fn warm(dir, cx)` uses `cx.background_spawn` to call `get(dir)`.
  - `pub fn get(dir) -> String` runs `OnceLock::get_or_init(|| print_prompt("piton", dir))`. Other threads block until the first run finishes, so the command runs once per project. There is no way to close a project, so "stays open" means for the life of the process.
  - `fn print_prompt(program, dir) -> String` runs `Command::new(program).args(["claude","--print-prompt"]).current_dir(dir)`. It returns stdout trimmed. On a spawn error or a non-zero exit it returns `""`.
- `init(cx)` follows the `ProjectLsp::init` pattern (`project_lsp.rs:36-49`): `observe_global::<ProjectDirectory>` calls `warm`, plus a `cx.defer` catch-up for a project set before the observer is in place.
- Test: `print_prompt("no-such-piton-binary", dir) == ""`.

### 2. `src/system_prompts.rs`
- Add `pub const PITON_FLUENCY: &str = "${PITON_FLUENCY}";` next to lines 19-20.
- `fill(template, code, spec, fluency)` (`:93`) also replaces `PITON_FLUENCY`, then `trim_end`s the result so an empty fluency leaves no trailing blank lines.
- Update the module doc (`:1-7`).
- Tests (`:103`):
  - Call `fill` with 4 arguments.
  - Assert every default contains the reference sentence and `ends_with(PITON_FLUENCY)`.
  - Assert the fluency text is filled in, and that `""` leaves nothing behind.

### 3. `.suspense/system-prompts/{code,combined,spec,ask}.md`
Append the following to each file. Leave the opening line alone: `hidden_anchor::mode_of` (`:500`) matches on the start of the prompt, so it keeps working.
```
Links to .claude/reference/… in the prompt are the spec for what they name. Read each one before changing anything it covers.

${PITON_FLUENCY}
```
Saved templates load as they are (`load`, `:62`), so older projects keep theirs with no migration.

### 4. `src/hidden_anchor.rs`
- `system_prompt(mode, project_dir, fluency: &str)` (`:487`) passes `fluency` to `fill`.
- It returns `None` when the *filled* text is blank. Otherwise a template holding only the placeholder, on a machine without piton, would send an empty prompt.
- Update the tests at `:764-786` (pass `""`) and `:932`.

### 5. `src/prompt_mode.rs` `resolve_anchor` (`:3539`)
- Call `hidden_anchor::system_prompt(mode, project_dir, &piton_fluency::get(project_dir))`.
- Every caller (`:1685` preview, `:1834` queue, `:1949` queue edit, `:2208` task, `:2419` question) already runs inside `background_spawn`, so blocking there never touches the UI thread. A prompt sent just after opening a project waits for the fluency.

### 6. `src/settings_window.rs:260-265`
Extend the description: "…{PITON_FLUENCY} stands for what `piton claude --print-prompt` prints in the project, or nothing without piton." Import the constant at `:18`.

### 7. Persisting the reset: `src/conversations.rs` (new)
- File: `.suspense/conversations.json`, holding `{"leftTasks": "<session id>", "leftQuestions": "<session id>"}` in camelCase (serde).
- Functions:
  - `enum Kind { Tasks, Questions }`
  - `pub fn left(project_dir, Kind) -> Option<String>`
  - `pub fn leave(project_dir, Kind, id: &str) -> Result<()>`
- Why store the id that was left rather than a flag: nothing ever has to clear it. After a reset, the next run reports a new id, so the stored one no longer matches the latest and the new conversation is carried on as normal. The button is disabled while a run is under way, so no older run can finish after the reset.

### 8. `src/prompt_mode.rs` conversation logic

- `load_history` and `load_answers` read `conversations::left` inside their background closures and pass it in. Keep the epoch guards.
- Rename `new_session` to `new_conversation` (`:2073`):
  - Return early unless the conversation can be reset (see below).

- **Placeholder:** templates now accept `${PITON_FLUENCY}`. It's filled with what `piton claude --print-prompt` prints in the project directory, run once in the background when a project is first opened and cached after that (new file `src/piton_fluency.rs`).
- **When `piton` is missing or fails:** the placeholder is filled with nothing. If a template ends up with nothing but blank space, no system prompt is sent at all.
- **Fluency not finished yet:** a prompt sent right after opening a project waits for it. The spec had said to send without it. I went with waiting because you asked for every run to start with it, and I changed the spec to match. There's no timeout, so a `piton` that hangs would also hold up that project's prompts.
- **Settings:** the note above the templates now explains `PITON_FLUENCY`. Saved templates are loaded as they are, so older projects keep theirs unchanged.

**3. New conversation**
- **Renamed, not added:** the last commit already put a "New Session" button in that spot, so I renamed it to "New conversation" instead of adding a second button.
